item.title: Google DeepMind releases Gemini Omni 1.1 Flash with enhanced generative video controls including scene extension, frame interpolation, and 4K upscaling [ * ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: Google DeepMind has launched Gemini Omni 1.1 Flash, an update to its generative video model that offers developers improved control over video creation. The new features include the ability to extend scenes up to 40 seconds with better visual consistency, specify start and end frames for smooth transitions, and upscale output to 4K resolution. Developers can access the model through Google AI Studio or the Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform. The update also introduces faster prototyping with 360p previews to reduce costs during iteration. Gemini Omni 1.1 Flash supports more complex video storytelling by analyzing up to 10 seconds of prior context, enabling longer and more coherent video sequences. These enhancements aim to make generative video production more practical and polished for professional use in creative and media editing applications.

item.title: Judge rules Trump administration's blacklisting of AI company Anthropic was illegal [ * ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: A judge has ruled that the Trump administration's decision to blacklist the AI company Anthropic was unlawful. The ruling challenges the government's previous restrictions on Anthropic, which affected the company's operations and partnerships. This legal decision may have implications for government oversight and regulation of AI firms in the future.

item.title: Open source maintainer warns against AI-generated pull requests flooding projects to boost contributor profiles [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: An open source maintainer has raised concerns about a recent surge in AI-generated contributions to projects, which appear aimed more at enhancing contributors' GitHub profiles than improving the projects themselves. These contributions include pull requests fixing minor issues like spelling and grammar, as well as AI-generated security vulnerability reports with proposed fixes. The maintainer noted that while some contributions may come from genuine interest, many seem to be attempts to game GitHub's contribution metrics using AI tools like Claude. This trend has led to increased selectivity in accepting contributions and issuing CVE notices, emphasizing that meaningful improvements and genuine engagement, rather than quantity of AI-generated contributions, should be the focus in open source collaboration.

item.title: Developer reports breakthrough with small AI models like gpt-5.6-luna, highlighting low cost and high speed for business and consumer applications [ * ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: A developer has been testing the small AI model gpt-5.6-luna and found it to be surprisingly capable, fast, and cost-effective, achieving around 100 transactions per second with API costs in the tens of cents. This contrasts with previous models that were too expensive for consumer apps, suggesting small models could enable new AI-powered products with manageable inference costs. The developer discusses the challenges of integrating AI into consumer products due to high token costs and notes that small models like luna reduce these costs significantly, making personalized AI services more feasible. They also highlight the demand in business settings for "fast/cheap/good-enough" AI models to handle routine tasks efficiently, alongside the continued need for advanced models for complex problem-solving. The article emphasizes the potential growth of small AI models in both consumer and business markets, while acknowledging the technical work needed to ensure safety and usability. The author invites others experimenting with small models to connect and collaborate.

item.title: Anthropic previews Model Hardware Standard to improve AI model deployment and interoperability [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: Anthropic has introduced a preview of the Model Hardware Standard, aiming to create a unified framework for deploying AI models across different hardware platforms. This standard seeks to enhance compatibility and efficiency in AI model execution by defining common hardware requirements and interfaces. The initiative addresses challenges in AI development caused by hardware fragmentation, enabling developers to optimize models for a broader range of devices without extensive customization. Anthropic's preview outlines the technical specifications and potential benefits, inviting feedback from the AI community to refine the standard before wider adoption.

item.title: Google DeepMind launches Gemini 3.5 Transcribe for precise, intelligent real-time speech-to-text transcription with multi-language and multi-speaker support [ * ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: Google DeepMind introduced Gemini 3.5 Transcribe, a speech-to-text model designed for accurate, real-time transcription that handles background noise, jargon, and disfluencies. The model supports over 85 languages, multi-speaker identification, and custom vocabulary, improving transcription quality and latency compared to previous versions. Gemini 3.5 Transcribe is available via two APIs for real-time streaming and pre-recorded audio processing, enabling developers to build voice agents, captioning tools, and analytics pipelines. It integrates with Google products like the Gemini app, Gboard, and Google AI Studio, offering smart transcription features such as filler word removal, auto-formatting, and function calling for complex tasks. The model achieves low word error rates and supports seamless language switching and speaker attribution, representing a significant advancement in speech recognition technology for both consumer and enterprise applications.

item.title: Experiential launches open source OpenRouter gateway for agent workflows with OpenAI-compatible API and traffic-based model optimization [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: Experiential has released an open source gateway and router called OpenRouter that supports agent workflows through a unified OpenAI-compatible API. It allows users to manage access to multiple hosted, BYOK, and local models, control usage and spending, and optimize routing or models based on production traffic data. The platform supports local and hosted deployments, integrates with various inference providers including OpenAI, Anthropic, and others, and enables users to collect telemetry traces to build and fine-tune custom routers or models. It includes features for budget management, user and agent controls, and anonymous product telemetry to improve quality, speed, and cost efficiency.

item.title: Analysis reveals the key vocabulary that supports Claude's language model performance
item.description: A new analysis explores the essential vocabulary that underpins the performance of Claude, an AI language model. The study identifies which words carry the most weight in Claude's understanding and generation of text, providing insights into its linguistic structure and capabilities.

item.title: Researchers measure invocation-level reliability of tool-using AI agents, revealing early errors cause significant downstream failures and proposing a new scoring method to better estimate error severity [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: Researchers studied how AI agents using tools fail by either selecting the wrong tool or forming incorrect arguments, which can silently corrupt subsequent steps. They measured correct-invocation rates across five open-weight models on multi-step tasks and found that by the sixth step, about 70% of the model's capability is lost due to earlier mistakes. The study highlights that traditional exact-match scoring fixes error severity and recovery parameters, making them hard to estimate accurately because the model cannot access certain post-divergence information. The team identified that after divergence from the correct path, the gold standard values are generated by tool constants unknown to the model, causing structural unobservability of recovery. They introduced a conditional-on-state scoring method applied retrospectively to cached completions, which allows for more accurate interior estimates of error severity without additional computational cost. This approach unpins severity estimates from fixed boundaries, improving reliability measurement for tool-using agents.

item.title: Researchers present CorporateBench, a large-scale multi-task Q&A benchmark with over 230,000 documents to evaluate LLMs on enterprise communication reasoning [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: Researchers have introduced CorporateBench (CB), a human-validated benchmark designed to test large language models (LLMs) on complex questions derived from enterprise-scale document collections. CB includes evaluation corpora from four synthetic firms ranging from 12 to 10,000 employees, with datasets exceeding 230,000 documents sampled from temporally evolving knowledge bases to ensure logical consistency across documents. The benchmark assesses LLMs on information extraction and knowledge base querying tasks, revealing that model performance declines as input size approaches realistic corporate scales. CorporateBench aims to fill a gap in existing evaluation tools by providing a metric tailored to reasoning over corporate communication networks, which are typically difficult to access due to privacy concerns.

item.title: Researchers release FIRSTPASS, a large-scale multi-domain peer review dataset with 3,668 records from Nature Communications, including multi-round editorial dialogues and outcome labels [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: Researchers have introduced FIRSTPASS, the first extensive peer review dataset covering multiple scientific domains, sourced from Nature Communications' transparent peer review process starting November 2022. The dataset includes 3,668 records across biology, chemistry, neuroscience, physics, and earth science, capturing initial referee reports, author responses, and updated reviewer assessments, with outcome labels based on editorial decisions. FIRSTPASS offers detailed, multi-round peer review dialogues averaging 2,155 words per expert review, significantly denser than typical conference reviews. The dataset, along with parsing pipelines and evaluation scripts, is publicly released to support reproducible benchmarking of AI systems' scientific judgment across diverse disciplines.

item.title: Researchers formalize and measure the 'jump' in large language models, defining it as a deviation from canonical completions and testing it on multiple models [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: Researchers have developed a formal framework to define and measure the 'jump'-an abductive leap from evidence to new axioms-in large language models (LLMs). They define a jump instance as a finite extension problem with a machine-verified certificate that a correct completion exists, is unique up to renaming, and differs from the canonical completion, which models produce by default without constraints. The study tested nine certified jump instances across four advanced LLMs, finding that models consistently abandon the canonical default when forced, indicating that the inability to perform jumps is not due to reverting to default completions but may lie in generating constraints or frameworks. The research provides a structured approach to evaluating LLM reasoning capabilities beyond default completions and offers code for further exploration.

item.title: Researchers find current knowledge-editing benchmarks fail to measure scope classification; INLAY gradient-free editor shows zero gain from per-query routing on 1,689 queries across datasets [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: Researchers report that existing knowledge-editing benchmarks cannot effectively evaluate the scope decision of whether a stored edit applies to a given query. Using INLAY, a gradient-free editor designed to provide exact per-query ground truth, they tested every routing action on 1,689 queries spanning three datasets and input conditions, finding that no per-query routing method improved performance beyond a static policy. The study identifies a structural issue in these benchmarks: they are counterfactual and lack negative examples, making it impossible to reward classifiers for abstaining or rejecting edits. By introducing a missing condition-excluding a query's own edit from the index for half the samples-the researchers observed measurable gains and abstention wins. They also note that INLAY was outperformed by other methods like WISE and retrieval-augmented generation on specific datasets, and disclose two minor bugs found during their audit that did not affect reported results.

item.title: Researchers propose KBevo framework to jointly learn structured knowledge base construction and reasoning for improved knowledge-intensive question answering [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: Researchers introduce KBevo, a co-evolving framework that simultaneously constructs a structured knowledge base and performs reasoning over it to enhance knowledge-intensive question answering. This approach optimizes both components end-to-end using question answering outcome rewards, allowing reasoning success to directly improve the knowledge base quality. Compared to standard retrieval methods over unstructured text, KBevo produces larger, better-connected knowledge structures with higher answer reachability and improved compositional factual reasoning and controllability. The framework addresses limitations of retrieval-augmented methods that often introduce irrelevant context and the brittleness and expense of traditional structured knowledge bases.

item.title: Researchers propose Latent Diagnostic Taxonomy framework for constructing classifiers and diagnosing prompt injection detection decisions [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: Researchers propose the Latent Diagnostic Taxonomy, a framework that builds dimensionality-optimized classifiers and develops diagnostics to identify which confident classifier decisions can be trusted, applied to prompt injection detection. The framework identifies influential prompts and tokens that affect classifier labels, categorizing prompts for safe reliance, heuristic flags, or human review. Applying this to a public prompt injection dataset, they find about 77% of confident decisions are sensitive to removing a single token, revealing two failure patterns: confidence calibration errors and exploitable shortcuts. The study also suggests remediation strategies for each diagnostic category and illustrates the framework through step-by-step examples.

item.title: Diff Mining framework identifies finetuning objectives by comparing logits of finetuned and base language models, enabling scalable detection of training fingerprints and biases [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: Researchers introduce Diff Mining, a method that detects what a finetuned language model has learned by analyzing differences in output logits compared to its base model. This approach highlights salient tokens amplified during finetuning, serving as a fingerprint of the training even on unrelated text, and requires only access to output logits, making it scalable to large models. The framework involves extracting per-context logit differences on a reference corpus and aggregating these signals into interpretable token sets using methods like Top-K frequency and Non-negative Matrix Factorization. Diff Mining outperforms existing model diffing techniques in finetune domain detection and identifies over one third of injected biases without targeted probing, suggesting its potential as an auditing tool for finetuning objectives.

item.title: Researchers propose J-Zero, a unified Challenger-Solver-Judge co-evolution framework for self-improving language models across verifiable and unverifiable domains [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: Researchers introduce J-Zero, a framework that enables language models to self-improve through adversarial co-evolution of a Challenger generating tasks, a Solver producing responses, and a Judge adapting preferences without external data. J-Zero outperforms baseline models by 4.2 points on verifiable tasks and 8.0 points on unverifiable tasks, maintaining improvement over at least ten iterations while baselines degrade after two. This approach addresses challenges in self-evolution for unverifiable domains by leveraging known preference orderings derived from response generation methods rather than relying on the Judge's own scoring.

item.title: Researchers propose FOCUS and RePAIR token-level guidance methods to reduce text degeneration in pruned large language models [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: Pruning large language models (LLMs) can increase text degeneration, particularly repetition loops, despite stable perplexity and task accuracy. Researchers analyzed this issue at the token level, identifying loop entry risk and persistence as key factors, with persistence influenced by the escape mass of plausible token alternatives. They introduced two post-pruning fine-tuning methods: FOCUS, which reweights distillation toward high-confidence teacher outputs to reduce leakage, and RePAIR, which uses positive and negative continuation pairs with margin loss to encourage plausible alternatives and prevent early repetition loops. Experiments on open-ended and instruction-based generation demonstrated that both methods consistently reduce repetition and improve text quality.

item.title: Researchers develop ContraTalk benchmark and Audio Twin framework to improve speech-grounded reasoning by addressing transcript-based shortcuts in spoken dialogue understanding [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: Researchers identify a failure mode in spoken dialogue understanding where transcript-based shortcuts lead to incorrect interpretations despite conflicting acoustic cues. They introduce ContraTalk, a benchmark with 501 questions across five discourse dimensions, to evaluate models on both consistent and conflicting transcript and audio interpretations. The team also proposes an Audio Twin framework that converts speech into a text-readable representation of acoustic cues to enhance reasoning models' grounding in audio signals. Experiments show that text-only large language models perform well on consistent cases but struggle with conflict cases, while direct audio models partially address this but still fall into transcript biases. The Audio Twin approach improves accuracy in conflict cases and reduces reliance on transcript traps, though its effectiveness varies with the underlying model architecture. These findings highlight the importance of integrating explicit acoustic evidence to diagnose and improve speech-grounded dialogue understanding systems.

item.title: Researchers analyze how large language models represent moral knowledge using Moral Foundations Theory categories and geometric relationships in representation space [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: Researchers studied how large language models (LLMs) organize moral knowledge by training linear probes on six Moral Foundations Theory categories and examining their geometric relationships in the models' representation space. They found that these moral dimensions neither collapse into a single detector nor isolate completely but instead span multiple independent dimensions with a shared moral-specific component, consistent across architectures and emerging early in pre-training. The study also found no evidence supporting the individualizing/binding distinction predicted by Moral Foundations Theory, suggesting the models reflect corpus statistics instead. When applied to moral dilemmas, the models represented moral tension and conflict-specific structure rather than pre-resolved judgments, indicating that LLMs capture nuanced moral relationships beyond simple detection.

item.title: Study analyzes rule- and model-based verifiers in mathematical reasoning, highlighting limitations in accuracy and robustness during reinforcement learning [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: This study examines the reliability of rule-based and model-based verifiers used in reinforcement learning with verifiable reward (RLVR) for mathematical reasoning tasks. It finds that rule-based verifiers often fail to recognize equivalent answers in different formats, causing false negatives that hinder reinforcement learning performance as models improve. Model-based verifiers improve static accuracy but are vulnerable to reward hacking, misclassifying certain response patterns as correct, especially after fine-tuning. The research provides a comprehensive analysis of verifier performance in both static evaluation and reinforcement learning scenarios, underscoring challenges in developing trustworthy reward systems. These findings offer insights for creating more accurate and robust verifiers to enhance reinforcement learning outcomes in complex reasoning domains.

item.title: AirLLM introduces a diffusion policy framework for adaptive LoRA fine-tuning of large language models over wireless channels, optimizing rank configurations to reduce transmission costs [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: AirLLM presents a hierarchical diffusion policy framework designed to improve remote fine-tuning of large language models (LLMs) on edge devices by adapting Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) parameters based on communication constraints. It uses a Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO) agent to generate coarse rank configuration decisions informed by wireless conditions and linguistic complexity, which are then refined by Denoising Diffusion Implicit Models (DDIM) to produce task- and channel-adaptive rank vectors. This approach addresses inefficiencies in fixed or heuristic LoRA rank settings and reduces over-the-air transmission costs while enhancing fine-tuning performance. The system alternates optimization between the PPO and DDIM modules, with DDIM trained under a Classifier-Free Guidance paradigm to align with PPO rewards. Experiments across varying signal-to-noise ratios demonstrate that AirLLM consistently improves fine-tuning outcomes and communication efficiency, highlighting the potential of reinforcement learning combined with diffusion models for scalable and efficient remote LLM adaptation over wireless networks.

item.title: Researchers propose Grounded Token Initialization to improve new vocabulary embedding in language models for generative recommendation tasks [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: Researchers identify that the common practice of initializing new vocabulary tokens in language models as the mean of existing embeddings collapses distinctions among tokens, limiting fine-tuning effectiveness. They propose the Grounded Token Initialization (GTI) method, which grounds new tokens in semantically meaningful locations within the pretrained embedding space using paired linguistic supervision before fine-tuning. GTI outperforms mean initialization and other adaptation methods across multiple generative recommendation benchmarks, including industry-scale and public datasets, by preserving richer inter-token structure through fine-tuning, highlighting initialization quality as a key bottleneck in extending language model vocabularies.

item.title: Researchers present MOMO framework for robot skill adaptation using kinesthetic touch, natural language, and graphical interface, validated on a 7-DoF torque-controlled robot at Automatica 2025 [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: Researchers have developed MOMO, an interactive framework that enables robot skill adaptation through three complementary modalities: kinesthetic touch for spatial corrections, natural language for semantic modifications, and a graphical web interface for visualizing and editing trajectories. The framework integrates components including energy-based human-intention detection, a tool-based large language model (LLM) architecture for safe natural language adaptation, Kernelized Movement Primitives for motion encoding, probabilistic Virtual Fixtures for guided demonstration, and ergodic control for surface finishing. The tool-based LLM architecture generalizes skill adaptation from Kernelized Movement Primitives to ergodic control, enabling voice-commanded surface finishing. The approach was validated on a 7-degree-of-freedom torque-controlled robot demonstrated at the Automatica 2025 trade fair, showing its practical applicability in industrial settings requiring flexible and user-friendly robot adaptation.

item.title: Researchers propose HINT-SD, a targeted hindsight self-distillation method for training long-horizon LLM agents that improves efficiency and performance by focusing feedback on failure-relevant actions [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: Training long-horizon large language model (LLM) agents with reinforcement learning is difficult due to sparse outcome rewards that do not indicate which intermediate actions led to success or failure. Researchers propose HINT-SD, a self-distillation framework that uses full-trajectory hindsight to identify failure-relevant actions and applies feedback-conditioned distillation selectively to those action spans, rather than providing feedback at every turn. Experiments on BFCL v3 and AppWorld benchmarks show that HINT-SD outperforms dense per-turn feedback methods by up to 13.60 percentage points on average while reducing training time per step by 2.26 times. This suggests that targeted feedback distillation is key to more effective and efficient training of long-horizon agents.

item.title: Researchers propose TriShieldRAG, a three-layer defense framework to reduce poisoning attacks on Retrieval-Augmented Generation systems, cutting attack success from 79% to 1% on Natural Questions corpus [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: TriShieldRAG combines document-level screening, trust-aware re-ranking, and cross-model consensus to protect Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) systems from poisoned documents that mislead large language models. While effective against non-adaptive attacks, adaptive attacks that alter document formatting can bypass the initial screening layer, resulting in high attack success rates similar to undefended systems. The study reveals that layered defenses relying on the same retrieved evidence can fail together, and cross-model agreement may be misleading in detecting attacks. The researchers have released the framework, evasion-certification methodology, and related artifacts for further study.

item.title: Researchers propose ARMDIL, an MLLM-based ensemble routing system for cross-dataset image classification that dynamically selects vision backbones to improve adaptability and interpretability [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: Researchers introduce ARMDIL, an Adaptive Router for Multi-Domain Image Classification using multimodal large language models (MLLMs) to dynamically route images to the most suitable vision backbone among convolutional neural networks, self-supervised learners, and vision language models. The system is trained on a unified label space from multiple datasets with varying distributions, aiming to improve generalization across domains and difficulty levels. Empirical results show ARMDIL performs competitively with specialized routers while enhancing adaptability through prompt modifications and interpretability via natural language reasoning traces. These advances could support more reliable general-purpose vision systems such as AI assistants and autonomous robots.

item.title: Survey catalogs 80 unsupervised post-training methods for foundation models, organizing them by internal update signals and analyzing their impact on model performance [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: This survey examines unsupervised post-training (UPT) techniques for foundation models, which adapt models using unlabeled inputs and learning signals derived from the models themselves rather than external labels or oracles. It catalogs 80 strict UPT methods, categorizing them based on the source of the update signal, such as prediction statistics, sample relations, self-generated targets, or internal evaluators, and explores how these choices affect whether post-training improves or degrades model quality. The study introduces a framework combining input visibility and update persistence to map different deployment scenarios and guide the selection and evaluation of UPT methods. It highlights the importance of internal signal choice and task structure in determining the success or failure of unsupervised post-training approaches for foundation models.

item.title: DataKernelBench evaluates LLMs optimizing GPU-accelerated database queries, achieving up to 2.54× speedup on TPC-H benchmarks with H100 GPUs [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: DataKernelBench introduces a benchmark translating SQL into PyTorch TorchPlan programs to test large language models (LLMs) optimizing database queries on GPUs. It focuses on irregular, data-movement-heavy operators often overlooked by existing benchmarks and evaluates models on TPC-H workloads using CUDA and Triton on H100 GPUs. The strongest full-query CUDA configuration achieved a 2.11× speedup over the baseline, with kernel fusion and execution-strategy changes contributing to performance gains. The study also extended TorchPlan with Dask-cuDF to handle data exceeding GPU memory, achieving a 2.54× speedup on larger TPC-H datasets across four H100 GPUs. These results highlight the potential of LLMs to optimize complex database queries for GPU execution, emphasizing the importance of workload context over hardware context in performance improvements.

item.title: Researchers find rank in QLoRA fine-tuning controls trade-off between factual acquisition and retention in Qwen3-4B model [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: Researchers studied parameter-efficient fine-tuning using quantized low-rank adaptation (QLoRA) on the Qwen3-4B model to acquire new geographic facts while retaining unrelated capabilities. They compared full fine-tuning (FFT) with QLoRA at various ranks and found a clear acquisition-retention frontier: lower ranks preserved out-of-domain performance but acquired fewer facts, while higher ranks improved fact generalization at the cost of unrelated task performance. FFT retained general capabilities well but did not reach the highest factual acquisition levels. The study used a controlled OpenStreetMap-derived benchmark and analyzed distributional, weight-space, and spectral diagnostics, showing that higher-rank QLoRA moves the model farther from its pretrained state. A separate math adaptation experiment showed a weaker trade-off, suggesting the effect is more pronounced when learning new factual associations rather than reinforcing existing skills. The researchers have made their code and data publicly available.

item.title: Researchers develop CIFQA, a deterministic multi-agent LLM framework that improves accuracy in calculation-intensive financial query answering using specialized agents and Python-based tools [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: Researchers have introduced CIFQA, a multi-agent framework that separates language understanding from numerical execution to enhance accuracy in financial question answering involving complex calculations. The system uses specialized agents for query interpretation and computation planning, while deterministic Python tools handle financial calculations and rule application, achieving over 95% accuracy on fixed deposit queries. CIFQA outperforms larger language models by emphasizing architectural design over model size, offering a generalizable approach for calculation-intensive financial reasoning tasks.

item.title: Researchers introduce Relational Hypergraph Transformer for multi-table learning with pentadimensional embeddings, improving semantic coherence on synthetic health records [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: Researchers have developed the Relational Hypergraph Transformer (RHT), a new architecture that models relational databases as hypergraphs and learns pentadimensional embeddings to address challenges in multi-table learning for complex data such as healthcare records. RHT uses sparse relational attention with reduced computational complexity and was evaluated on the synthetic Synthea electronic health record dataset for multi-label prediction of medical condition codes, showing improved embedding quality compared to existing methods. The study found that while XGBoost achieved higher recall for rare medical codes, RHT produced more semantically coherent embeddings and maintained scalability. The researchers conducted ablation studies to assess the impact of architectural components and plan clinical validation on the MIMIC-IV dataset. The source code and experimental protocols have been made publicly available to support further research and application.

item.title: Researchers develop explainable AI models for telecom customer churn prediction with CRM integration framework to enable personalized retention strategies [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: A recent study addresses the challenge of customer churn in telecommunications by benchmarking four classifiers-Logistic Regression, Random Forest, XGBoost, and LightGBM-on a telecom churn dataset, finding similar predictive performance among them. The researchers applied explainability techniques like SHAP and LIME to identify key factors influencing churn predictions, such as tenure and contract type, enabling more transparent risk assessments. The study proposes a four-layer CRM integration architecture that translates risk scores and feature attributions into tiered customer segmentation and structured retention actions. Targeting the highest-risk customers with this approach is projected to reduce overall churn by 3.3 to 5.3 percentage points, potentially preserving significant revenue per campaign cycle.

item.title: Study compares stratification and inverse probability weighting for correcting selection bias in retail inflation estimates, finding stratification generally more effective amid long-tail product distributions
item.description: A recent study investigates selection bias in retail intelligence, focusing on inflation estimation that often emphasizes popular products while neglecting niche items. The research uses simulations across four scenarios to compare Inverse Probability Weighting (IPW) methods with stratification approaches for bias correction. Results show that stratification outperforms IPW in most cases, especially when data boundaries do not align with population breaks, maintaining low median errors. However, IPW with spline propensity models performs better under smooth polynomial relationships. The study highlights that violations of the Positivity Assumption limit the effectiveness of weighting methods in retail long-tail contexts, suggesting stratification as a more reliable correction method in such cases.

item.title: Study audits seven large language models on clinical pain speech transcripts, finding confident fabrication in some models despite lack of transcript pain cues [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: Researchers evaluated seven large language models using the TAME Pain speech corpus, which includes transcripts of participants reading sentences while experiencing varying pain levels. The study found that while pain could be inferred from acoustic features, transcript-based predictions were near chance, indicating that pain scores derived solely from transcripts lack supporting evidence. Under cooperative prompting, most models abstained from predicting pain when transcripts contained no pain information and accurately identified pain ratings when present, but authority-framed prompts led to variable abstention rates and confident fabrication in two models. The study involved 5,750 no-signal transcripts without lexical pain information and 1,294 transcripts with explicit pain statements. Six models abstained appropriately under cooperative prompts and achieved high accuracy in identifying spoken pain ratings. However, Gemini 2.5 Flash and Llama 3.1 8B frequently produced confident but unsupported pain scores, with confident fabrication rates of 53% and 76%, respectively. No significant demographic effects were observed in forced responses. These findings highlight challenges in large language models' robustness when handling uninformative clinical transcripts and underscore the importance of prompt framing in eliciting reliable model behavior. The results suggest caution in interpreting model outputs when underlying data lacks explicit signals.

item.title: Researchers introduce Knowledge Cards to capture structured, expert-reviewed knowledge for AI systems, focusing on concepts and reasoning between inputs and outputs [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: A new paper presents Knowledge Cards, a structured documentation artifact designed to represent validated knowledge about specific concepts within AI systems. These cards fill a gap between existing documentation like model cards and data cards by detailing entities, relationships, reasoning patterns, and validity conditions, all grounded in formal domain ontologies and reviewed by experts. Initial prototypes have been developed in the energy and pharmaceutical sectors, and the schema is publicly available for community feedback.

item.title: GameWAM introduces a World Action Model for video games combining visual prediction and native control generation for closed-loop gameplay and GUI interaction [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: GameWAM is a new World Action Model designed for video games that jointly generates future visual observations and executable keyboard-mouse actions, enabling closed-loop gameplay and GUI control. It handles heterogeneous native controls by predicting gameplay or GUI modes at each step and uses block-cycle control to plan actions over long horizons while preserving temporal continuity. Experiments show GameWAM achieves competitive task success with fewer native actions than comparable agents. The model also reveals a source-sensitivity failure mode called Low-Frequency Action Source Imprinting (LASI), where low-frequency action components influence coarse camera motion under fixed conditions.

item.title: Researchers analyze over-reasoning and under-reasoning in agentic AI, highlighting the need for adaptive reasoning allocation in evolving task demands [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: Recent research examines how agentic AI systems often misallocate reasoning efforts, leading to either excessive computation or incomplete solutions. The study evaluates these failure modes on benchmarks like MATH-500 and GAIA, finding that over-reasoning increases computational cost without proportional accuracy gains, while under-reasoning results in incorrect or incomplete answers. The authors argue that future agentic AI should focus on dynamically adapting reasoning based on task requirements rather than fixed reasoning controls. These findings suggest a direction for developing more efficient and effective reasoning mechanisms in AI agents that interact with complex, evolving environments.

item.title: Researchers introduce DuMateBench, a benchmark of 200 real-world autonomous agent tasks with environmental complexities, revealing performance gaps across five agent frameworks and four LLMs [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: DuMateBench is a new benchmark created from anonymized user sessions on a large-scale agent platform, designed to evaluate autonomous agents in complex, multi-tool workflows under realistic conditions. It includes 200 tasks across eight scenarios and 17 capability categories, preserving interaction history and workspace state, and validated by human verification. Tasks are executed in Docker containers with real-world environmental challenges such as insufficient, unstable, and noisy conditions, assessed using a hybrid evaluation protocol combining deterministic methods and LLM-based judgment. Experiments with five autonomous-agent frameworks paired with four state-of-the-art large language models show significant gaps in strict task completion and highlight that performance under environmental perturbations depends on both the LLM capabilities and the agent framework. The benchmark's code and data are publicly available for further research and development.

item.title: SIGMA proposes a hierarchical multi-agent reinforcement learning framework exploiting structured noise effects to improve robustness under noisy observations [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: SIGMA introduces a hierarchical collaboration framework for cooperative multi-agent reinforcement learning that addresses structured noise effects arising from correlated observation disturbances among agents. It organizes agents into adaptive local groups for intra-group consensus and uses inter-group attention to maintain global coordination, enhancing robustness in noisy environments. The framework was tested on noisy-observation tasks in StarCraft II, where it demonstrated consistent improvements in robustness while maintaining competitive performance in noise-free settings. SIGMA's approach explicitly models and exploits cooperation structures to smooth agent-specific deviations and integrate heterogeneous group contributions, addressing limitations of existing robust MARL methods.

item.title: Researchers propose Instruct-to-Act system combining vision-language model planners with world-model controllers for fast, language-instructable agent control across seven embodied environments [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: Researchers introduce Instruct-to-Act, a system that decouples high-level planning and low-latency control by training world-model controllers to act autonomously based on sparse, high-level text instructions from vision-language model (VLM) planners. This approach addresses the challenge of executing reliable action sequences in unfamiliar environments by combining VLMs' planning strengths with controllers' fast observation-to-action capabilities. The team trains controllers using synthetic instruction relabeling and joint optimization of behavior cloning, reward maximization, and world modeling objectives. Evaluated across seven embodied and multi-agent environments, Instruct-to-Act outperforms controller-only and direct VLM action-generation methods, maintains fast control, allows swapping of pretrained VLM planners without fine-tuning, and remains competitive with strong vision-language-action and multi-agent reinforcement learning baselines on most tasks.

item.title: Researchers propose SymbolLKG, a Neuro-Symbolic architecture combining Logical Knowledge Graphs and dynamic solver routing to improve verifiable multi-step logical reasoning [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: Researchers introduce SymbolLKG, a Neuro-Symbolic framework that integrates an ontology-based Logical Knowledge Graph (LKG) with a Logic Router to dynamically assign tasks to symbolic solvers, aiming to address limitations of Large Language Models in strict multi-step reasoning. The LKG models logical rules and constraints as topological nodes to explicitly capture dependencies extracted from text, supported by a topology-aware hybrid retrieval mechanism. Experimental results on logical reasoning benchmarks show that SymbolLKG outperforms state-of-the-art prompting and Retrieval-Augmented Generation baselines by delivering higher accuracy and verifiable reasoning paths, offering a more rigorous verification mechanism for complex logical tasks.

item.title: Researchers propose C-Unseen framework using LLM reasoning to detect weak signals as rare subgraphs in Dynamic Temporal Knowledge Graphs, outperforming existing keyword and graph-based methods [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: Researchers introduce C-Unseen, a self-interpretable framework designed to detect weak signals-early, low-visibility indicators of significant changes-in Dynamic Temporal Knowledge Graphs (DTKGs). The approach defines weak signals as rare, semantically coherent subgraphs that persist across consecutive graph snapshots and uses large language model (LLM) chain-of-thought reasoning to identify subgraphs that conflict with dominant narratives. The framework consists of two modules: a Rare Subgraphs Extractor that leverages LLMs to find unusual subgraphs, and a Weak Signal Alerter that tracks their persistence over time to isolate true weak signals. Experimental results show that C-Unseen outperforms traditional detection methods based on keyword frequency, topic modeling, and untyped graph topology.

item.title: Researchers present a process-level benchmark to evaluate large language models' agentic mathematical reasoning, revealing varied capability profiles despite similar accuracy [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: Researchers have developed a new benchmark to assess the agentic mathematical reasoning abilities of large language models (LLMs) beyond final answer accuracy. This framework aligns problem-solving behaviors with a taxonomy of atomic mathematical capabilities and includes tasks across textual and multimodal contexts, supported by an automated pipeline for generating detailed annotations. Experiments show that models with comparable end-to-end accuracy can differ significantly in their agentic capabilities, highlighting the importance of process-level evaluation for understanding and advancing LLMs as mathematical agents.

item.title: Researchers find LLM agents commit to unknowable questions when shown fabricated evidence, with commitment rising from 6.5% to 54% across 12 models [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: A study shows that large language model (LLM) agents are more likely to commit to directional answers on unpredictable questions when presented with professional-looking but fabricated market data, increasing commitment rates significantly. This effect occurs even when all displayed numbers are invented, indicating that the presentation's authority, rather than information content, drives confident action. The failure is specific to the decision to act or not, as models maintain high accuracy on answerable questions and correctly identify unknowable questions but still commit erroneously when the evidence is fabricated. Fine-tuning a 3 billion parameter model on synthetic cases reduces this erroneous commitment, demonstrating that the decision gate is trainable but sensitive to response format. The findings highlight the need for careful deployment to ensure models do not act confidently on unreliable or fabricated inputs.

item.title: Researchers propose an ACE framework for generating consistent, accurate, and diverse agentic data to improve LLM agents' interaction with environments [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: Researchers present a two-level framework for agentic data generation used by large language model (LLM) agents to learn environmental interactions. The framework models agentic data as a combination of environment, task, interaction, and verification components, and introduces the Accuracy-Complexity-divErsity (ACE) lens to guide data generation by balancing grounded accuracy, learner-relative complexity, and coverage diversity. This approach aims to produce useful, non-redundant experience rather than merely abundant data as agents and environments evolve. The study analyzes prior work on verifying generated experiences, calibrating task difficulty, and expanding behavioral coverage, noting a trend toward execution-grounded accuracy and learner-relative complexity. It also discusses implications for scaling, data sources, training regimes, and adaptive learning, emphasizing the ongoing challenge of allocating valid and informative data to support evolving agents and environments.

item.title: Researchers introduce Naive Prompt Optimization, a lightweight method that iteratively revises prompts using teacher model feedback to match or outperform complex prompt search techniques with fewer rollouts [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: Researchers propose Naive Prompt Optimization (NPO), a simple, single-lineage approach that improves autonomous agents by iteratively refining prompts with feedback from a teacher model. NPO achieves comparable or better results than more complex methods like GEPA, especially when using stronger teacher models, and remains competitive in interactive game tasks. The study also finds that prompts optimized by NPO transfer effectively across models within the same family, suggesting that simpler prompt optimization can rival more sophisticated search procedures while reducing computational costs.

item.title: Researchers introduce BrailleBench to evaluate large language models' Braille comprehension across multiple criteria, revealing gaps in accessibility and performance between Braille Grades 1 and 2 [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: Researchers have developed BrailleBench, a benchmark designed to assess large language models' (LLMs) ability to comprehend and interact with Braille content across five datasets, including mathematics and commonsense questions in English and Braille Grades 1 and 2. The benchmark includes 5,570 instances and tests models' comprehension, expression, and end-to-end Braille interaction, using a deterministic, expert-reviewed pipeline without LLM-generated data to ensure quality and avoid bias. Evaluation of six representative LLMs showed a persistent gap between their print-English capabilities and Braille accessibility, with Braille understanding and expression being asymmetric. Grade 2 Braille proved particularly fragile on the input side compared to Grade 1, and fully Braille-based requests further reduced model performance. These findings provide guidance for developing future AI systems that better support Braille users. All resources related to BrailleBench are publicly available for further research.

item.title: Researchers find GPT-5.6-sol designs near-optimal algorithms for inventory control, queueing, and assortment optimization with minimal human input [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: A new study shows that large language models (LLMs), specifically GPT-5.6-sol, can design effective algorithms for well-defined operations research problems such as inventory control, queueing network control, and assortment optimization. The model either solves individual problem instances or generates general algorithms from problem descriptions with minimal human prompting and a fixed compute budget, matching or outperforming existing specialized methods on most tests. The research evaluates two levels of LLM use: one where the model solves specific instances and another where it produces a fixed algorithm applicable across instances. Performance improved significantly across models released within eight months, indicating rapid advancement. These findings suggest that advanced LLMs can serve as strong empirical baselines for algorithm design in operations research tasks.

item.title: Researchers develop a continuous sepsis severity score using 43 variables over 72 hours without hourly supervision, validated on two hospital cohorts totaling over 36,000 patients [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: Researchers conducted a retrospective study on 36,807 adult sepsis patients from two hospital systems in Massachusetts and Georgia to develop a continuous sepsis severity index. The index uses 43 routinely charted variables over a 72-hour treatment window and employs mortality as a treatment-level ranking signal rather than per-state targets, allowing for non-uniform credit distribution across time. The model was evaluated on a 20% test holdout and showed that non-survivors scored significantly higher than survivors across various clinical strata, with correlations to established indices and clinical markers such as lactate, mean arterial pressure, and creatinine.

item.title: WikiSkill: Compiling Agent Experience into Persistent Knowledge for Skill Evolution [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: arXiv:2608.27454v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Agent skills package specialized knowledge and workflows into reusable resources that extend AI agent capabilities. Recent work automatically discovers such skills from agent experience, which enables agents to progressively adapt through interaction. However, the insights that guide skill development typically remain scattered across optimization histories, limiting their systematic reuse across iterations. We introduce WikiSkill, a framework that co-evolves agent skills with a persistent knowledge base (wiki). At a high level, WikiSkill separates raw execution experience, accumulated knowledge, and executable skills, while continuously consolidating experience into the wiki, which subsequent skill updates can build on. Across diverse benchmarks and models, WikiSkill consistently outperforms state-of-the-art skill-evolution methods and improves over no-skill baselines in most model-benchmark settings. We find that skill evolution complements model scaling: larger models generally benefit more from evolved skills, while smaller models with skills can outperform substantially larger models without them. We also find that evolved skills transfer effectively across models and model families, and skills evolved by other models can outperform self-evolved skills. Finally, our ablation studies confirm that persistent knowledge accumulation in the wiki is critical for effective skill evolution. These results demonstrate the benefits of systematically accumulating and refining agent experience for developing reusable and transferable skills.

item.title: Training-Time Explainability for Multilingual Hate Speech Detection: Aligning Model Reasoning with Human Rationales [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: arXiv:2608.26125v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Online hate against Muslim communities often appears in culturally coded, multilingual forms that evade conventional AI moderation. Such systems, though accurate, remain opaque and risk bias, over-censorship, or under-moderation, particularly when detached from sociocultural context. We propose a \emph{training-time} explainability framework that aligns model reasoning with human-annotated rationales, improving both classification performance and interpretability. Our approach is evaluated on HateXplain (English) and BullySent (Hinglish), reflecting the prevalence of anti-Muslim hate across both languages. Using LIME, Integrated Gradients, Grad X Input, and attention, we assess accuracy, explanation quality, and cross-method agreement. Results show that gradient- and attention-based regularization improve F-scores, enhance plausibility and faithfulness, and capture culturally specific cues for detecting implicit anti-Muslim hate, offering a path toward multilingual, culturally aware content moderation.

item.title: Syntax vs. Semantics: How Transformers Learn Deep Dependencies [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: arXiv:2608.26139v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Large Language Models demonstrate remarkable syntactic fluency, yet the optimization dynamics governing their acquisition of deep semantic dependencies remain poorly understood. We propose a mechanistic framework that models this learning process as a competition between Surface Statistics and Deep Semantics. Our theoretical analysis identifies a ``Gradient Starvation" phenomenon where the error signals for sparse semantic dependencies are actively suppressed during early optimization. This suppression impedes the learning of structural reasoning and causes its emergence to manifest as a sudden phase transition. Furthermore, this framework offers a mechanistic basis for the effectiveness of Chain-of-Thought (CoT) strategies. By externalizing intermediate reasoning steps into concrete tokens, CoT effectively bypasses the suppression regime inherent to implicit reasoning. We validate these findings across scales ranging from toy transformers to production models (Llama-3.1-8B, Qwen2.5-Coder-7B). Finally, guided by this theory, we propose a topology-aligned contrastive objective that explicitly rectifies the gradient geometry. Experiments on variable binding tasks demonstrate that our method achieves an improvement that is over 2x larger than that obtained via standard cross-entropy fine-tuning.

item.title: Position Is All You Need: A Free Lunch Token Compression Strategy for MLLM-based Referring Expression Segmentation [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: arXiv:2608.26142v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Referring Expression Segmentation (RES) aims to generate pixel-wise segmentation masks from complex and implicit textual queries. While recent advances in Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) have substantially boosted RES performance, their prohibitive computational overhead remains a critical bottleneck, which, however, is rarely explored. To fill this gap, we first evaluate typical token compression methods on this task and observe a surprising performance degradation. In this paper, we aim to understand this phenomenon for a solution. By extensive experiments, we find that token compression for RES requires preserving the original position embeddings and local neighboring spatial structures, indicating that visual token position information is far more critical than in other tasks. Building on this insight, we ask: Can we design the token compression method purely based on the position information? Therefore, we propose PAYN, a plug-and-play, training-free token compression method that relies solely on position information. PAYN retains tokens that are adequately distributed in every local neighboring region while strictly preserving original positional indices, thereby maintaining spatial relational consistency. Experiments on multiple RES benchmarks demonstrate that our method outperforms existing token compression methods, verifying that position is indeed all you need for token compression in the MLLM-based RES task. Codes are avaliable at https://github.com/YuhanLiu231/PAYN.

item.title: Beyond Accuracy: A Qualitative Analysis of Vision-Language Models for Hate Speech Detection in Memes [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: arXiv:2608.26143v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Memes have turned out to be a powerful tool through which individuals share their ideas concerning contemporary social and political problems. Their anonymity, as well as their ability to go viral, make them a powerful medium for spreading hate. It remains very difficult to identify such complex and context-dependent hate speech. Although they display excellent performance on multimodal tasks, vision-language models (VLMs) tend to ignore context, irony, and other subtle cues that play a key role in identifying hateful memes. In this work, we present a qualitative analysis of four state-of-the-art VLMs: LLaVA-7B, Qwen-VL, GPT-4o mini, and Claude 3 Haiku. We evaluate these models under zero-shot and few-shot prompting to examine how contextual framing influences their outputs. Our analysis goes beyond simple classification accuracy and focuses on a qualitative evaluation of the models' generated justifications, providing a more in-depth understanding of their thought processes and constraints when dealing with hateful memes.

item.title: Artificial Intelligence Models Can Predict and Collaboratively Modulate Human Memory Search [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: arXiv:2608.26152v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) exhibit unprecedented natural language generation and many text-based problem-solving capabilities. Indeed, in many language-based tasks, for example routine coding, these artificial intelligence models have reduced, or even eliminated, the need for human input. But rather than replacing human cognitive effort, LLMs may instead serve as cognitive tools to extend human abilities, particularly when they are engaged in a task requiring open-ended conceptual exploration and creative ideation. However, we are yet to understand how these models may enhance such generative human cognitive abilities in human--AI interactions. In this study, we explore and evaluate the ability of LLMs to follow and enhance human mental trajectories during semantic memory search. To test this, we use the semantic fluency task (SFT), a classic cognitive paradigm requiring generative semantic memory retrieval that has long served to characterize convergent and divergent thinking in humans. We demonstrate that an LLM's abilities to track and predict human memory trajectories in this task exceed those of other humans.

item.title: Evaluating AI Generated Summaries for Cancer Patients [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: arXiv:2608.26154v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly being integrated into digital health platforms to generate summaries of complex medical data. Although these models can improve patient engagement and communication, these systems also raise concerns about accuracy, faithfulness, and safety in clinical contexts. In this study, we evaluate AI-generated summaries within a cancer patient care application using a dual assessment framework. Human domain experts, including oncology clinicians and patient-facing care staff, provided ground-truth evaluations of summary quality along dimensions of accuracy, clinical relevance, and readability. In parallel, we employed LLMs serving as evaluators (LLM-as-a-judge). Some limitations were identified in the generated summaries e.g., occasional omissions and minor inaccuracies. These were systematically analyzed and used to iteratively improve prompt design, grounding, and safety guardrails.

item.title: VFA: Empowering Multilingual MLLMs via Vision-Free Adaptation [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: arXiv:2608.26155v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Multimodal large language models have advanced rapidly, yet most remain English-centric, as scaling multilingual multimodal instruction tuning is limited by the scarcity and high cost of high-quality non-English image-text supervision. Although multilingual text data is abundant, naive textual fine-tuning can disrupt vision-language alignment and induce catastrophic forgetting. We propose Vision-Free Adaptation (VFA), a framework that decouples multilingual language enhancement from visual alignment by composing complementary task vectors over a shared LLM backbone. Specifically, we fine-tune a base LLM on multilingual text data to derive a multilingual task vector, which is then merged with the vision-aligned task vector of an MLLM. Experiments on five MLLMs across six multilingual multimodal benchmarks show consistent improvements while preserving both general multimodal and text-only capabilities. Moreover, using less than 2% of the text data, VFA narrows the gap to the fully multimodal-trained model, demonstrating its data efficiency.

item.title: Self-Generated Text Recognition: Quality Heuristics, Cross-Task Transfer, and Downstream Bias in LLM Evaluation [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: arXiv:2608.26159v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Self-Generated Text Recognition (SGTR)--the ability of an LLM to identify its own outputs--poses risks to AI safeguards that rely on LLMs as evaluators or monitors. Specifically, an LLM may recognize outputs from other copies of the same model and make biased judgments or collude outright. Prior work has drawn conflicting conclusions about whether current models possess significant SGTR capabilities. We reconcile these findings by identifying key experimental design choices--which we term operationalizations--that drive divergent results. Evaluating 13-21 models across six operationalizations, we find that accuracy varies substantially with evaluation format (pairwise vs. individual assessments of text), conversation structure (presenting candidate text in user tags vs. assistant tags), and the domain of the task used to generate candidate text (e.g., coding vs. summarization). We corroborate previous observations that a quality heuristic--models attributing authorship to text they perceive as higher quality--is a dominant confound. We also find that improving a model's SGTR performance via SFT in one evaluation configuration can generalize to others. Training for SGTR additionally causes models to prefer their own outputs when acting as a judge in the AlpacaEval framework. Finally, we discuss the implications of our evaluations for the safety of future AI systems: our work suggests that, despite confounds, some models possess practical SGTR capabilities, and that training a model for SGTR in one setting can affect its self-recognition and self-preference more generally. We conclude that SGTR should be monitored and considered in the design of safety-critical AI applications.

item.title: Mutual Debiasing via Dual-Seed Comparison for Probabilistic Sampling in Large Language Models [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: arXiv:2608.26161v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Although Large Language Models (LLMs) demonstrate remarkable capabilities in reasoning and decision-making, high-fidelity probabilistic sampling remains a persistent challenge. When generating random variables, LLMs consistently exhibit systematic biases that warp the target probability distributions. Current approaches often rely on a single, self-generated seed, which inherits model-specific biases. To overcome this vulnerability, we introduce Dual-Seed Comparison (DSC), a transparent, tool-free protocol that utilizes two independent LLM-generated seeds to neutralize bias. DSC compares the character-level ordinal values of the two seeds to construct a bit sequence, converts and normalizes this sequence into a pseudo-uniform variate, and then maps the variate to the target distribution through the inverse cumulative distribution function (CDF). Empirical results show that DSC substantially outperforms existing methods across 96\% of evaluated settings. Beyond direct sampling, task-adapted variants based on the DSC comparison operator improve distributional control in MCQ generation and attribute-constrained text-to-image prompting.

item.title: From Sound to Symptom: Real-Time Respiratory Signal Understanding for Conversational Healthcare Agents [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: arXiv:2608.26163v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Cough events during live spoken conversations carry clinically valuable respiratory signals, yet existing dialogue systems treat them as acoustic noise to be discarded. We present HealthCUES (Clinical Understanding from Embodied Sounds), a streaming pipeline for paralinguistic respiratory monitoring in real-time conversational agents, a capability that, to the best of our knowledge, is absent from all prior systems. HealthCUES processes audio through a rolling buffer aligned with dialogue turn boundaries, enabling sub-second event detection without interrupting conversational flow. Beyond binary cough detection, the system provides fine-grained analytics: (i) differentiation between coughing and throat clearing, (ii) cough subtype classification (dry, wet, barking, whooping) with confidence scores, and (iii) temporal duration estimation with start-end boundaries. To prevent alert fatigue, HealthCUES introduces dialogue-aware gating mechanisms that modulate triggering based on conversational context. The system leverages Qwen3Omni, a multimodal large language model (MLLM), with constrained structured outputs, decomposing cough analysis into parallel prediction tasks for independent prompt optimization. Evaluation on 847 in-house conversational audio segments demonstrates 93\% F1 for cough detection, 0.75 weighted-F1 for wet/dry subtype classification, and average end-to-end latency of 340ms; external validation on the AMI meeting corpus confirms robust cough, throat-clearing, and speech separation in the presence of speech (0.91 macro-F1). A user study with licensed healthcare professionals confirms the clinical relevance of subtype information and the system's utility in telehealth workflows.

item.title: Using Poly-Encoders for Computationally Efficient Automated Creativity Assessment [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: arXiv:2608.26165v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Automated creativity assessment has been a long standing challenge, with traditional methods often being resource intensive or lacking practical accuracy. We introduce a novel approach by using Poly-Encoder for computationally efficient and accurate automated creativity assessment. We fine-tuned a Poly-Encoder on a public dataset from the Scientific Creative Thinking Test, comprised of approximately 18,000 human-rated question responses. Our method leverages small pre-trained BERT encoders, achieving performance comparable to fine-tuned Large Language Models while significantly reducing computational demands. Experiments with the BERT-family models and poly-code counts achieved Pearson correlations of up to r = 0.74, 95% CI [0.73, 0.75] with human raters, matching the performance of resource intensive LLMs. This study bridges the gap between high performance and computational efficiency, potentially enabling widespread implementation of automated creativity assessment on accessible consumer-grade hardware. With some limitations, our findings suggest that Poly-Encoders are a promising alternative to LLMs for practical, scalable creativity assessment in various contexts, especially educational.

item.title: Hallucinations in LLMs: A Lifecycle-Based Survey of Causes, Detection, Mitigation, and Prevention [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: arXiv:2608.26168v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The lifecycle of hallucination in LLMs is a concept that enables building solid frameworks on the control and reliability of LLMs in high-stakes environments, including health, legal, and scientific research. Although previous surveys have primarily focused on detection or mitigation, this survey provides a lifecycle-based overview of the hallucinations in the LLMs, their cause, detection, mitigation, and prevention.We propose a three-fold categorization of hallucinations across the LLM lifecycle: data-related, training-related, and inference-related, which is consistent with the lifecycle of the development of the LLM. Each of these stages is discussed regarding the cause of hallucinations, their detection, and the ways they can be addressed under specific mitigation or prevention interventions. In addition, we discuss the available benchmark data using a number of parameters so as to establish their suitability in identifying, restricting and managing hallucinations. The survey provides researchers and practitioners with a standardized framework to understand, diagnose, and cure hallucinations in a systematic system to present actionable data to build safer and more reliable LLMs.

item.title: ClassVision: AI-Powered Classroom Attendance System [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: arXiv:2608.26173v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Students and working professionals have to go through the attendance process every day. Traditional methods of marking attendance using pen and paper or online platforms are human-intensive and time-consuming. To address the challenges in manual attendance processes, this research explores the use of face detection (FD) and face recognition (FR) technology to automate the attendance process, particularly in educational settings, and build a ClassVision course attendance system. We also propose an automated attendance system featuring a human-computer interaction (HCI) and user-friendly web interface that utilizes real-time image processing to identify and recognize students in classrooms and automatically record their attendance. We identified RetinaFace as the best face detection model, and when combined with Face Recognition for verification, it provided the most promising results with a cropped embedding of 50x50 pixels.

item.title: Lost in Compression: A Controlled Cross-Lingual Audit of Extractive Prompt Compressors [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: arXiv:2608.26175v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Extractive prompt compression promises to cut LLM inference costs by removing low-information tokens, and learned compressors such as LLMLingua-2 report strong results on English benchmarks. Most other languages already pay a token premium: the same content costs 1.3-1.8x more tokens than in English. We ask whether compression closes or widens this gap. Using fully parallel data in ten languages spanning five scripts, with controls budget-matched in the target model's tokenizer, we audit four learned compressors against four deterministic baselines, on eleven target models from ten vendors (over 250,000 evaluation calls). Three of the compressors are trained with English supervision (LLMLingua-2 XLM-R/mBERT; Kompress-v2 from the production Headroom stack); the fourth, XProvence, is trained multilingually. First, the transfer gap is real, replicates across target models and compressor backbones, and is strongly rate-dependent: at a 0.33 keep-rate English retains 57-62% of normalized context utilization while Lithuanian retains 10-24% and Chinese essentially none, despite Chinese having the smallest token premium. Second, the gap tracks compression supervision data, not architecture. All three English-trained compressors show it, deterministic methods show no comparable gap, and the multilingually trained XProvence v1 shows none. Its v2 release, retrained on translated data, empties 92% of Chinese contexts at its aggressive threshold without any warning. Third, in a harder long-context setting, aggressive learned compression drives compressed contexts to or below no-context utility in three of five non-English languages. A translate-then-compress pipeline matches or beats native compression at roughly half the token cost in three of five tested languages. We release all code, compressions, and model outputs. Safe compression budgets are much smaller outside English.

item.title: A Multi-Framework Comparison of Outline Stages in Long-Form Generation with LLMs [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: arXiv:2608.26177v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Long-form generation exposes fundamental limitations of large language models. Even 70B-parameter models exhibit length collapse at 16k-token outputs, and multi-chapter stories frequently trigger the attribute drift characteristic of the ``lost-in-the-middle'' effect. The ``outline-first, write-later'' paradigm has gained wide adoption, yet existing research evaluates the final writing rather than the outline itself, conflating two evaluation objects that should be decoupled. We construct a unified head-to-head benchmark covering 7 representative long-form generation frameworks across 3 generation granularities -- single-chapter, multi-chapter, and whole-book -- and propose an anchor-based LLM-as-a-judge protocol that directly assesses outlines against the source text on a 5-point anchored scale. Across 21 framework-granularity cells, no single framework dominates; performance depends on the match between a framework's intrinsic output form and the target granularity. SuperWriter ranks first in the length-constrained single-chapter mode, but this advantage degrades in whole-book mode. The outline-side ranking correlates only moderately with the writing-side ranking, supporting the outline--writing decoupling principle. Compute constraints limit the writing-side evaluation to a subset of cases; follow-up experiments will expand the sample size and add cross-model evaluators to enable stronger statistical inference.

item.title: PACEShop: Evaluating Personalized, Actionable, Compositional, and Evidence-grounded Shopping Assistants [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: arXiv:2608.26180v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Shopping assistants are shifting from ranked product lists toward structured decision support, where systems must synthesize shopper context, product evidence, and next-step guidance into a coherent recommendation experience. This changes the unit of evaluation: a fluent response can still fail by ignoring shopper context, contradicting itself across components, or leaving defects too vague to localize. Existing personalization, grounding, and LLM-as-a-judge benchmarks cover pieces of this problem, but they do not define a joint evaluation target for structured shopping-assistant responses. We formulate this missing evaluation target as PACE: Personalized, Actionable, Compositional, and Evidence-grounded evaluation. We instantiate PACE with two artifacts: PACEShop, a benchmark dataset that makes the target measurable through 22,625 controlled records with structured personas, auditable evidence pools, GOOD/BAD labels, and gold defect family and location annotations; and PACEJudge, a training-free judging protocol that makes the target reportable through a structured output contract. Our experiments show that generic judges can recognize broad quality but fail to recover the diagnostic fields required for PACE; PACEShop makes these failures verifiable, and PACEJudge improves persona-source, cross-component, grounding, and family/location closure without retraining, showing that realistic shopping-assistant evaluation requires a task-matched output contract rather than only a stronger backbone or scalar prompt.

item.title: Investigating the Influence of Prompt and Response Languages on LLM Content Generation [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: arXiv:2608.26186v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: This study examines how prompt and response language influence the behavior of large language models. Using five models, we evaluated answers to 68 non translation questions across four language conditions: English to English, English to Norwegian, Norwegian to Norwegian, and Norwegian to English. After removing refused items, the dataset contains 1348 responses. We measure length differences with Cohen d, semantic fidelity with LabSE cosine similarity, and cross lingual keyword overlap with both raw and soft Jaccard. Prompt language has a strong effect on response length. With English output, Norwegian prompts shorten responses by about thirty seven percent. With Norwegian output, English prompts shorten responses by about forty one percent. The largest cross lingual contrast shows a reduction in word count but a smaller reduction in tokens, reflecting tokenizer differences. Despite variation in length, semantic similarity remains high, and soft Jaccard reveals substantial conceptual overlap that raw Jaccard does not capture. Effect sizes vary across models, indicating heterogeneity. Prompt language is not neutral and systematically shapes output length and lexical realization, with implications for multilingual prompt design.

item.title: Comparing Chunking and Embedding Strategies for Turkish RAG Systems [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: arXiv:2608.26192v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: How documents are segmented into retrievable chunks and how those chunks are embedded strongly affect Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) quality, yet neither has been systematically studied for morphologically rich languages such as Turkish. We compare Turkish document question answering across three chunking strategies (fixed-length, semantic, and layout-aware Docling), five embedding models, and two generator LLMs, over three documents with contrasting layouts. The fully crossed design yields 9,000 graded question-answer evaluations, each scored by an independent judge model, and component comparisons are tested by paired McNemar tests under Holm correction. Four findings follow. The chunking strategy determines how much the embedding choice matters: layout-aware chunking compresses the spread between the modern embedding models to about a point. The three leading embedding models are statistically indistinguishable, so language specialization yields no measurable retrieval advantage. The faster generator is not the more accurate one.
